transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah. Um, well, I guess I should start by saying I've been thinking about coming in for a while now. Because, you know, being 19 and trying to figure things out... I'm actually taking some time off from college right now, so I have a lot of time on my hands, and my eating habits just kind of got really, really out of hand. 

But what really made me actually pick up the phone and come in today is... well, it's what happens when I eat sometimes. It's like, once I start eating like that, it feels like I hit some switch in my brain and I just keep going. And it's the most frustrating thing in the world because I'll be sitting there, and I keep going, even while a huge part of me is actively thinking, 'Dennis, just stop already.' Like, I'm literally telling myself in my head to quit, but my hands just keep moving and grabbing more, you know? It's like I'm watching myself do it from the outside and I can't intervene. I just can't stop once that switch flips, no matter how much I argue with myself. So I just felt like I really needed to talk to someone about why my brain is doing that.
When you say you can't stop eating once it starts, does it feel like a complete loss of control, like you're unable to stop or resist the urge to keep eating even though you want to?

Yeah, exactly. It's... it's a total loss of control. It's so bizarre because, like I said, I'm fully aware it's happening. It's not like I zone out and then suddenly realize, 'Oh, I ate all this.' No, I'm right there, in the moment, and my internal monologue is just screaming at me. I'll be sitting on the couch, or sometimes standing right in front of the pantry with the door open, and I'll have, say, a bag of chips. And I'll eat a handful, and then another, and then my brain is like, 'Okay, Dennis, that's enough, you're not even hungry, put the bag away.' But my hand is already reaching back in. 

It's like... it's like my body is operating on completely different instructions than my brain. I'll even try to physically force myself to stop, like I'll tell myself, 'Just close the bag, just roll down the top.' But I can't do it. I just keep eating and eating until the bag is empty, or until I feel so sick I physically can't swallow another bite. And the whole time, I'm just so angry with myself. I'm sitting there thinking, 'Why are you doing this? You don't want this.' But the urge to keep going is just... it's overwhelming. It completely overrides any rational thought or willpower I have in that moment. It's incredibly scary, honestly, feeling like you're a passenger in your own body like that.
Do these episodes cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your daily life, like affecting your relationships, school, or how you see yourself?

Well, um, it's... it's kind of a mix, honestly. Like, I wouldn't say it's completely ruining my life or anything dramatic like that. I'm still functioning, you know? Even though I'm taking time off from regular college classes, I'm still taking a couple of online courses just to keep my mind sharp, and I'm still going to my robotics club meetings. I've been in robotics since high school, and I really love it, so I haven't let this stop me from doing that. I'm still showing up, building things, working with the team. 

But... it does bother me. It bothers me a lot, actually. It's more of an internal thing, I guess. Like, if I have one of those episodes at night, the next morning I just feel... ugh. I feel so sluggish and gross, and my stomach is usually upset, which makes it really hard to focus on my online lectures. I'll be sitting at my desk, trying to listen to a video about, I don't know, introductory physics or something, and my mind is just completely elsewhere. I'm just replaying what happened the night before, feeling guilty and angry at myself. 

And then there's the whole thing with my roommates. I live with two other guys, and I spend so much time worrying if they've noticed. I mean, I try to be quiet when I'm in the kitchen late at night, but what if they heard me? What if they noticed that half a box of cereal is suddenly gone, or that the trash can is full of wrappers? I'll literally spend twenty minutes analyzing how I threw away a chip bag just to make sure it's buried under other trash so they won't see it. It's exhausting. It just takes up so much mental energy, you know? So, yeah, it hasn't completely knocked me off track or stopped me from doing the things I need to do, but the distress it causes me... the worrying, the guilt, the feeling like I'm hiding this huge, shameful secret... that's the part that really gets to me. It's just a constant weight on my mind, even if I'm still managing to get my work done.
After these episodes of eating, do you ever try to compensate by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising excessively?

No, I... I don't do any of that. I mean, I know some people do that kind of thing, like throw up or whatever, but that's never really been my thing. I hate throwing up, actually. Like, even when I was a kid and I'd get the stomach flu, I would fight it for hours because I just despise the feeling of being sick like that. So the idea of doing it on purpose? No way. 

And as for laxatives, I don't even know where I would buy those, to be honest. I guess at the pharmacy, but I've never even looked down that aisle. And fasting... well, obviously that's not really working out for me, considering the whole reason I'm here. I might wake up feeling so full and gross that I think, 'Okay, I'm just not going to eat today,' but by the time 1:00 or 2:00 PM rolls around, I'm hungry again, or at least my brain thinks I am, and I end up eating anyway. So I can't even stick to a fast if I try. 

And exercising... I mean, I like robotics, which involves some walking around the lab and carrying metal parts, but I'm definitely not a gym guy. I don't go running or lift weights or anything. Sometimes I'll think, 'Oh, I should go for a walk to burn off what I just ate,' but it usually just ends up being a ten-minute stroll around the apartment complex before I get bored and go back inside. So, no, I don't really do anything to... compensate, I guess you'd call it. I just kind of sit there with the guilt and the uncomfortably full stomach and just wait for it to pass, which usually takes until the next day. It's just a cycle of doing it and then feeling terrible about it, but not actually doing anything to physically undo it, you know?
How often do these episodes happen? Like, how many times a week or month would you say you experience that loss of control while eating?

Well, um, let me try to trace it back, because it’s kind of a blur sometimes when I try to look at the whole picture. But if I really think about it... it really started becoming a regular thing early in the semester. You know, right around when classes were just getting underway and everyone was settling into the apartment routine. 

My roommates, they have this habit of going to the store and just buying massive amounts of snacks—like, those huge bulk boxes of chips and cookies and whatever else—and they just pile it all up in the pantry. So the food is always just... there, staring at me every time I walk into the kitchen. Anyway, since early in the semester, I'd say it’s been happening most weeks. Usually, it's just one night a week. I'll be up late, the apartment is totally quiet, and it just happens. 

But then, sometimes it bumps up to two nights in a week. That usually happens when I have a bunch of deadlines hitting all at once for my online classes. Like, if I have a big project due and I'm stressed out and staring at my laptop for hours, or if the guys just did a huge grocery haul and the apartment food pile is just overflowing, that's when it's way more likely to be twice a week. I just get so overwhelmed by the stress of the assignments, and then knowing there's a mountain of junk food sitting ten feet away from me just makes it impossible to ignore. 

So, yeah, usually one, sometimes two nights a week. And if I look at the calendar... I mean, early in the semester was a while ago now, so I’d say that exact pattern—the one or two nights a week thing—has been pretty steady for at least the last three or four months. It's just been this constant, exhausting cycle for months now, week in and week out, just totally depending on how much homework I have or how full that pantry is.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports recurrent episodes of binge eating without compensatory behaviors, occurring at least once a week for several months. The episodes are associated with marked distress and a sense of lack of control. There is no evidence of purging, fasting, or excessive exercise after eating, which rules out bulimia nervosa (F50.0). The clinical picture aligns with binge eating disorder (F50.2).

inference_history.note: The patient describes a loss of control over eating, which points towards a potential eating disorder. Candidates include F50.2 (Binge Eating Disorder), F50.0 (Anorexia Nervosa), and F50.9 (Eating Disorder, Unspecified) as specific diagnoses under eating disorders in the ICD-10. No other categories were ruled out yet, and further details are needed to narrow down the diagnosis.

The patient's distress is primarily related to the loss of control during eating episodes and associated guilt/shame, rather than significant impairment in daily functioning or body image concerns. This makes F50.9 less likely. F50.2 and F50.0 remain due to the described binge eating behavior and associated psychological distress.
